sections.eyebrow: THE JASPER FIELD SEMESTER / ACADEMIC CURRICULUM
sections.title: Strong in body. Free in mind.

blocks.html: A six-week education in physical capability, independent thought and useful creation. Learn in person in Jasper, Alberta, through field practice, science, philosophy and a small community of inquiry.

blocks.alt: Spirit Island and Maligne Lake in Jasper National Park

blocks.html: Understanding demonstrated through responsible action.

Proposed non-degree program | 6–8 adults aged 18+ | 144 facilitated + 24 independent-study hours. English edition: 15 October 2026. General inquiries are welcome at vincent@ujasper.ca. Formal admissions and appointments are not open. Website forms prepare local drafts and never submit automatically; a draft is not an application, reservation or offer.

To unite sustained physical training, humanistic learning across world civilisations, and original inquiry in mathematics, physics, chemistry and economics. Through life in nature, lectures, close dialogue, debate, field study, experiments and shared projects, we cultivate people of courage, deep learning, independent judgment, initiative, self-discipline and a commitment to justice. We use AI to extend inquiry while strengthening human understanding, creativity and responsibility.

blocks.text: What this semester must make possible

blocks.html: Learners should be able to care for themselves and companions outdoors; train with control; direct attention voluntarily; measure and reason from evidence; interpret texts and challenge arguments fairly; and complete useful work with others.

Physical practice develops capability and judgment. World humanities examine purpose and responsibility. Mathematics, physics, chemistry and economics make explanations precise and testable. Jasper’s setting connects the work; disagreement remains welcome.

The long-term mission includes thoughtful use of AI. The six-week core establishes an independent record of observation and reasoning offline. Personal phones, internet and live AI are off during teaching and camps, with agreed private medical, accessibility and essential-contact exceptions. Staff emergency communications remain active. Storage is voluntary and devices are returned on request. An optional three-hour AI Return Lab follows separately, outside the 168 academic hours; no seventh residential week is promised.

High expectations apply to preparation, precision, honesty, revision and care. Distance covered, combat dominance, meditation endurance, obedience and agreement with the founder are not measures of worth.
Fearless in learning. Lead by example. One University → One Family means mutual care with freedom to disagree, decline a practice or leave the program.

blocks.html: Total: 144 facilitated learning hours = 24 days × 6 hours. Weekly allocation: fieldcraft 6; martial arts 3; attention 2; science 5; philosophy 5; commons 3. Course codes are internal design labels, not accredited credit codes.

Adults aged 18 or over; cohort of 6-8; no martial-arts experience required. An opening diagnostic checks arithmetic, graph reading, short-text comprehension and support needs. It shapes teaching and adaptations, not a public ranking.

Four teaching days provide 24 facilitated hours weekly. Four additional independent-study hours cover reading, essay development and laboratory preparation: 24 over six weeks, making 168 planned academic hours in total. Guided reading and writing also occur in class. Camp duties, meals, breaks and travel are additional commitments, not hidden teaching hours. No full residential provision is promised.

blocks.html: Each day ends at 16:15. Every day contains exactly 360 teaching minutes and 75 minutes of meals/breaks. Field breaks may be redistributed by the lead; access, weather and health needs take priority over the clock.

Winter break: mid-December to mid-February, approximately two months. No required teaching or camping takes place during this period. Six-week cohorts finish before the break or begin after it. Exact cohort dates remain unconfirmed.

In camping weeks use A on Tuesday, C on Wednesday, B on Thursday and D on Friday. Week 2 has one night; Week 5 has two nights, with Saturday checkout. Evening attention may replace the Day C 60-minute attention seminar only when staffing, darkness and recovery arrangements are confirmed. The hour is moved, never added or counted twice.

Three days have no scheduled contact teaching; four independent-study hours are planned separately. Camp rest and duty need their own staffing. Night-sky work is optional or replaces an existing attention hour. Keep an approximately nine-hour sleep opportunity at camp.
A shared question connects physical effort, scientific reasoning, primary texts and contribution. Each component stays within its course allocation.

blocks.text: Warmth / What does it take to keep someone warm?

blocks.html: Jasper’s mountain conditions make warmth a question about physical preparation, heat transfer and shared responsibility. Create a tested preparation resource for a consenting user. Show the evidence behind each recommendation and revise what the user misunderstands.

blocks.text: Water / Where does the water go?

blocks.html: Medicine Lake opens a question about hidden systems, chemical evidence and the limits of what we can know. Produce an annotated water-system model for a consenting reader. Make the uncertainty understandable rather than hiding it.

blocks.text: Judgment / What would change your mind?

blocks.html: A difficult text, an uncertain measurement and a real responsibility test the same capacity: judgment. Complete useful work for a consenting peer or confirmed host. Defend your contribution; optionally audit AI against the preserved work after the semester.

Count each session once under its scheduled course. A field observation can supply a science question, but it cannot also be claimed as a second block of teaching hours. The learner’s portfolio makes the connections visible.
Jasper is the setting for a proposed program, not an approved laboratory or booked campus.

sections.eyebrow: SIGNATURE INQUIRY / FROM WATER TO JUDGMENT
sections.title: Where does the water go?

blocks.html: Use Parks Canada’s account of Medicine Lake and an approved local observation or printed site material. Draw what is visible, what is inferred and what remains unknown. The basin is a problem to understand, not a place for unauthorized sampling.
Write a water balance with storage, inflow, outflow, precipitation and evaporation. Mark the units and the measurements you would need. Compare two possible explanations for a changing lake level.

Analyse the published Miette ion concentrations. Convert units, compare molar quantities and explain why a partial mineral list is not a complete water analysis. Distinguish this published dataset from anything you measured.

Use a selected primary argument about knowledge and action or shared resources. Ask what a community may reasonably decide when its knowledge is incomplete. Defend a view in tutorial and answer a serious objection.
Produce an annotated model or explainer for a consenting reader. Test whether they can tell facts, assumptions and unknowns apart. Revise it and defend your own reasoning.
This sequence draws on existing science, philosophy, fieldcraft and Commons sessions. Full sources and data-preparation requirements appear later in this curriculum.
Use five dimensions, scored 0-3. Apply the same standards to equivalent adapted tasks. Provide the rubric before teaching, descriptive feedback in Week 3 and a revision opportunity in Week 6.

head: Dimension
2: competent for this introductory course
3: strong independent evidence
rows: Practice & care
Prepares, observes boundaries, adapts load and acts reliably.
Anticipates needs and helps peers without taking over.
Evidence & reasoning
Uses units, sources and a defensible method; names limitations.
Tests alternatives and explains consequences of uncertainty.
Interpretation & argument
Cites a passage, reconstructs an opposing view and answers it.
Makes a precise distinction and revises after a strong objection.
Original work & revision
Makes a useful artefact, tests it and documents a revision.
A peer can reproduce or use it; revisions improve demonstrated quality.
Contribution & autonomy
Keeps an agreed commitment; respects consent and dissent.
Creates fair conditions for others to contribute and choose.

blocks.html: Level 0: evidence absent or task not yet demonstrated. Level 1: partial evidence requiring substantial prompts. A high score in one dimension does not cancel a missing safety-critical demonstration.

Submit six weekly entries, two revised essays, a scientific dossier and useful original work. Reach level 2 in each dimension after revision; demonstrate required field and martial stop procedures. Complete physical practice records and an individual defence. Address missing work through documented equivalents. Award only a descriptive non-credit record.

Assess what learners can show, not personality, confidence, physique, spiritual experience or agreement with a doctrine. Allow oral, written, diagrammatic and adapted demonstrations. A second educator reviews disputed assessments.

blocks.html: Encounter something directly. Form a question before consulting authority. Make a model or argument. Try to disprove it. Ask a peer to challenge it. Revise it. Give the resulting knowledge or work a practical use.

blocks.text: One example across all six courses

blocks.html: A cold morning prompts a field decision about clothing and shelter. Science compares heat retention. Mathematics makes a graph. Philosophy asks what hardship is for. Martial practice tests restraint under effort. Meditation notices a response without demanding endurance. The commons project produces a tested, readable packing guide.
Every week must leave a trace of changed judgment, not merely a memory of attendance. The final work should reveal how the learner grew and what still needs study.

Develop physical capability and field judgment together. Practise strength with a qualified coach, prepare and navigate an approved outing, share camp responsibilities and lead a bounded part of a culminating field mission. Explain the evidence behind an adjustment.

Two competent field staff for the proposed group of eight, as a design minimum rather than a universal legal ratio. The responsible guide sets a lower ratio if required by the route, participants, insurer or authorization. Use licensed local guiding arrangements where required and instructors whose qualifications match the terrain. [S2, S3]

The first program uses maintained non-technical routes and frontcountry camping. The culminating mission combines preparation, navigation, sustained appropriate effort, observation and shared leadership. Exact routes, loads and progression are set for the actual group by the responsible lead. See the companion manual for operating boundaries.

30 minutes coached strength and movement; 15 route/camp briefing; 95 guided travel or campcraft; 25 observation or decision work; 15 debrief. The separately scheduled 30-minute field break is not instruction. Twelve blocks provide 6 strength hours and 30 other field hours. Rearrangement for the approved setting must preserve these totals.

Move from an individual baseline and sound technique toward repeatable practice, greater appropriate challenge and shared leadership. The coach can progress movement quality, range, repetitions or resistance as appropriate. The guide progresses field responsibility. More load, remoteness or speed is never automatic.

A private baseline and retest record, twelve coached practice entries, a route-and-camp dossier, observed preparation and a justified field decision. Demonstrate a progression appropriate to you and explain the part you played in the group mission.

sections.eyebrow: JAS 101 / SIX HOURS WITHIN THE FIELD COURSE
sections.title: Strength with a purpose

blocks.html: Build a sustainable practice in moving, carrying and controlling the body. Twelve 30-minute sessions provide deliberate coaching within the 36-hour field course. They support field capability and do not claim a guaranteed physical transformation in six weeks.

5 minutes private readiness check and warm-up; 5 demonstration and rehearsal; 15 practice with rest and feedback; 5 recovery and a brief record. Choose an appropriate subset of supported squat/sit-to-stand, hinge, push, pull, carry and trunk-stability patterns. Equipment and variations depend on the qualified coach and venue.

blocks.text: A baseline that belongs to the learner

blocks.html: In Week 1 the coach selects two or three submaximal tasks and records the movement, support, load if used, repetitions or time, technique and self-reported effort. No maximal lifts, timed exhaustion test or public ranking. Repeat comparable tasks in Week 6 and record changes in conditions.

Consistent practice, sound technique at an appropriate challenge, responsiveness to feedback and a reasoned progression. Strength numbers are private evidence, never measures of character or a required universal threshold. An adapted task can meet the same learning outcomes.
The coach writes individual variations and stop decisions. This curriculum is not a personal exercise prescription. Staffing, equipment and operational procedures are in the companion manual.

blocks.html: Week 5 brings two authorized camp nights and supervised leadership on an approved daytime route. The group produces a route plan, shares roles, completes one observation and revises a decision. Each learner explains a choice that mattered; staff retain route and safety authority.
Tasks progress individually. Do not infer a training effect from a better result without considering familiarity, technique, conditions and other explanations.

Use a staff-approved short local route. Record ten observations, three inferences and one uncertainty. Read legend, scale and orientation at three agreed stops. Evidence: A sketch with orientation, units and an observation/inference distinction.

At the venue, compare two printed route plans and test a packed-kit checklist. Practise a regroup and a plain-language help message without leaving the supervised area. Evidence: A route card with turnaround time, exit options and named responsibilities.

At a reserved serviced campsite, practise shelter setup, layout, dry storage and shared chores. The lead teaches the site’s actual food and wildlife procedures. Use staff-approved cooking equipment only. Evidence: A camp layout and witnessed food/attractant check; no food stored in sleeping space.

After the first camping night, complete a short guided walk or an accessible observation circuit. Compare predicted and actual clothing, sleep and equipment needs; pack out and leave the site clean. Evidence: Three adjustments justified by experience, not a public sleep or toughness score.

Choose an approved route with simple observation stops. Measure sections against the printed map; explain why pace, grade and weather change a time estimate. Evidence: A revised time estimate with a range and a stated limitation.

The guide presents a tabletop change in weather, pace or access. Learners choose proceed, shorten, move indoors or cancel and communicate their reasons. No unsafe situation is staged. Evidence: A decision record showing evidence, alternatives and who may veto departure.

Pairs explain the next short section while the guide retains control. Rotate leader, navigator, companion-check and recorder roles. Keep the party together. Evidence: A map-based explanation and a peer check, not an unsupported navigation claim.

Compare two camp layouts on paper and set up approved shelter on permitted ground. Examine wind, drainage, accessibility and shared space without digging, cutting or building structures. Evidence: A labelled plan with two trade-offs and an accessible alternative.

Repeat the readiness gate. Set up in a reserved serviced site; assign fair chores, verify communications and practise the agreed regroup location. Evidence: A signed camp plan and private access arrangements; no automatic remote progression.

Complete the culminating field mission from the authorized camp. Learners take bounded leader, navigator, companion-check and recorder roles on an approved route. Integrate one scientific observation and a real resource decision. Evidence: A justified adjustment, a contribution record and a debrief distinguishing individual and group work.

Repeat the coach-selected submaximal baseline tasks and revisit a comparable route or map problem. Record support, load, technique, conditions and perceived effort privately. Evidence: Explain physical and decision-making changes without treating speed or strength as character.

In the supervised venue, teach a peer one approved field skill, check their understanding and revise the handout. Finish with a leave-no-trace audit of the actual learning space. Evidence: A usable instruction sheet and a witnessed teach-back.

Develop disciplined effort, balance, technical understanding and restraint through a qualified coach’s introductory martial practice. Discuss Kanō’s principles of efficient effort and mutual benefit as one educational influence. The initial format uses controlled footwork and pad work; a judo variant requires a separate coach-approved plan and suitable facilities.

Use a qualified, insured martial-arts coach with current first aid and a clear safeguarding process. Inspect floor, spacing, mats and cleaned shared equipment. Match partners by consent, size, experience and comfort. Touch, partner changes and intensity each require agreement. Observing, solo practice or an adapted movement task earns equivalent learning evidence.

No head strikes, hard sparring, knockouts, chokeholds, neck cranks, joint submissions, weapon work or uncoached takedowns. Floor exercises require suitable mats and a coach competent to teach them. No technique is taught on a trail or beside a fire. Do not claim the course makes a learner safe in a real assault.

5 minutes readiness and consent; 15 warm-up; 20 coached technique; 25 controlled practice; 15 stop-signal, pacing and recovery work; 10 journal and peer teach-back. Rest and adaptation occur throughout. Stop immediately for pain, dizziness, distress or loss of control.

Acknowledge the partner’s consent, maintain an agreed pace, respond immediately to stop, explain one mechanical principle and reflect on restraint. No grading by winning a bout or enduring discomfort.
Practise posture, spacing, footwork and a verbal stop cue with a coach. Use solo movement before any paired task. Evidence: Explain where balance is lost and demonstrate an immediate stop.
Use slow pad-target work or a solo equivalent selected by the coach. Notice stance recovery rather than power or speed. Evidence: A coach checks alignment and a learner names a correction.

On suitable mats, use coach-chosen low-resistance balance tasks; no throws or submissions. Partners continuously agree the level of contact. Evidence: Relate base of support to the science lesson without claiming a universal fighting rule.
Repeat a short coach-set practice at a conversational effort where appropriate. Learners choose and explain rest intervals. Evidence: A personal pacing plan with a reason to reduce or stop.
Watch a short technical demonstration and distinguish what was seen from what was inferred. Practise the selected correction slowly. Evidence: Two observations and one testable technique question.
One learner practises, one observes a single coach-approved cue, then they change roles. Feedback is specific and consent-based. Evidence: Describe one improvement without comparing people’s bodies.

Rehearse assertive verbal boundaries, stepping away and seeking help through non-contact scenarios. No simulated ambush or coercive role-play. Evidence: Clear communication and a decision to disengage.
Use a predictable coach-led cue change during solo footwork or pad practice. Learners stop, reset and describe what changed. Evidence: Control and responsiveness, not reaction-speed ranking.
Design a short safe sequence from previously approved movements, then have the coach review it before practice. Evidence: A sequence card with purpose, stop conditions and adaptations.
Explain one approved movement to a peer under the coach’s supervision. The coach corrects any unsafe instruction. Evidence: A clear cue, a check for understanding and a correction accepted.
Practise the final sequence at an agreed pace. Show the solo or adapted equivalent. Include a stop and restart decision. Evidence: Feedback against the published control criteria.

Complete a three-minute coached demonstration, explain one physics connection and discuss one decision to exercise restraint. Evidence: Coach-reviewed evidence; no belt, fighting licence or professional credential.

Learn to notice distraction, choose an attention method and return to a task. Each week has four 15-minute opening sessions and one 60-minute seminar: two hours weekly, twelve in total. Meditation is one available method, alongside quiet drawing, attentive walking, reading or sensory orientation.

2 minutes: offer choices and notice comfort. Up to 10 minutes: selected practice, beginning with shorter intervals in early weeks. At least 3 minutes: write one observation and choose an intention. Unused practice time becomes orientation or journalling, not pressure to sit longer.

“Choose a comfortable seated or standing position. Eyes may remain open. Notice an ordinary sound, a visible object or natural breathing. When attention moves, notice that and choose where to place it next. You may change the practice, stop or step out.” Do not direct unusual breathing, breath holding or pain endurance.

10 minutes of context and choice; 10 of practice or an equivalent; 15 comparing observations; 15 discussing an idea; 10 designing a personal protocol. Keep personal disclosures voluntary. The instructor never interprets someone’s distress as necessary progress.

Use a facilitator trained to offer short, accessible practices and respond appropriately to distress. This is education, not psychotherapy or treatment. Stop or change an uncomfortable exercise; offer private support and appropriate referral when needed. Evidence on benefits and adverse effects is mixed, so no clinical promises are made. [S6]

Explain how a method affects your own attention, distinguish an observation from a belief, and make a reasonable adaptation. Stillness, closed eyes, spiritual experiences and willingness to disclose are not graded.

Use 3-5 minute intervals within the opening. Compare attending to a sound and to a visible object. Seminar question: When did attention change? What did you observe rather than assume? Evidence: A private two-column observation/inference note; share only a chosen example.

Use up to 5-7 minutes if comfortable, or stay with shorter intervals. The seminar compares a rigid rule with a flexible, repeatable practice. Seminar question: Can discipline include changing the plan? Evidence: A protocol with a preferred method, duration, alternative and stop condition.

Compare quiet reading with attentive observation on separate occasions. Keep setting and task similar where practical. Seminar question: Does one experience justify a general claim about everyone? Evidence: A short method comparison with confounders and no health conclusion.

Invite a private check-in, not a compulsory emotional disclosure. Record attendance or the chosen equivalent; do not retain intimate journal content. If a practice is not helpful, changing it is an acceptable result.
The shared university vision protects independent thought. A meditation instructor’s authority never extends to requiring a worldview, secrecy, isolation or unquestioning obedience.

Use paired listening: two minutes speaking, two listening, then a faithful restatement and a check. Silent presence is optional. Seminar question: Can I understand a position before preparing my reply? Evidence: A restatement the speaker recognises as fair.

Study the night sky from an approved supervised location when conditions and staffing permit. Record three observations, one inference and one uncertainty; compare attention to a star chart with attention to the actual sky. Use a daytime printed-sky session if necessary. The 60-minute seminar is rescheduled, not added, and camp sleep remains protected.

Try the preferred method for up to 10 minutes; shorter or non-meditative alternatives remain equally valid. Design a realistic continuation. Seminar question: What helps me return to worthwhile work? Evidence: A 30-day plan without a promise of transformation or mandatory reporting.

Invite a private check-in, not a compulsory emotional disclosure. Record attendance or the chosen equivalent; do not retain intimate journal content. If a practice is not helpful, changing it is an acceptable result.
The shared university vision protects independent thought. A meditation instructor’s authority never extends to requiring a worldview, secrecy, isolation or unquestioning obedience.

Use Jasper’s sky, water, landscapes and shared resources to build models and test explanations. Mathematics supplies scale, geometry, rates, uncertainty and dimensional reasoning. Physics and chemistry explain mechanisms; economics examines choices. Every learner must defend a model, an alternative and a limitation.

Use three challenge levels within each investigation: Foundation reconstructs units and a supplied model with prompts; Standard independently analyses evidence and tests one alternative; Extension examines sensitivity, compares competing models or derives an additional prediction. All levels require source honesty, a defensible conclusion and individual explanation. Support changes access, not the obligation to reason.

15 minutes: individual prediction. 20: model and method discussion. 45: investigation. 25: calculation and graph. 25: peer challenge or replication. 20: revise and write an exit claim. Include safety checks within instruction; scheduled breaks remain outside these minutes.

Printed Jasper maps and sources; dated glacier imagery with usable scale; a star chart; published Miette mineral values; site diagrams; rulers, protractors, string, ordinary thermometers and low-risk tabletop apparatus. The educator must assemble and verify the source pack before enrolment. Label every illustrative dataset.

Label every datum with a unit or category; preserve original measurements; record repeated trials, relevant controls and limitations. A failed prediction can be excellent work. Illustrative datasets in this guide are invented for teaching and must never be presented as Jasper field measurements.

Submit an 800–1,200-word scientific dossier or agreed equivalent, with an attributable dataset, calculations, a model, a competing explanation and uncertainty. Keep raw notes. A peer audits the method; each learner defends the reasoning individually. Permission to deliver the actual field activities must be established separately.

How does a representation shape a journey? Use a licensed or reusable Jasper map with date, scale and legend. Make five independent measurements of a short segment; convert to ground distance. Read the published account of Samson Beaver’s map used by Mary Schäffer in 1908. Distinguish precision, cultural knowledge and the limits of a printed representation.
Mathematical demand: Scale, ratios and uncertainty. Extend to alternative route geometries and an uncertainty range.
Evidence: An annotated map, repeated measurements, source credit and a written limit. Maps support learning; staff approve routes separately.

What can we infer without reaching a summit? Estimate a fixed feature’s height from an approved observation point or an indoor model. Compare similar triangles with angle-and-baseline geometry. Record slope, observer height and assumptions. Use a Jasper landscape image with a valid scale only when the geometry supports measurement.
Mathematical demand: Similar triangles; tan(theta) = height difference / horizontal baseline. Derive and critique the construction.
Evidence: Two estimates, a diagram and a sensitivity check. No approach to cliffs or water edges is needed.

blocks.text: 3 / The sky as a coordinate system

blocks.html: How could the sky help us find direction? Use a sourced star chart and Jasper’s latitude to construct horizon and celestial diagrams. Explain Earth’s rotation and a circumpolar star’s apparent path. If a supervised observation is feasible, record time and conditions. Otherwise work from the printed chart, labelled as such.
Mathematical demand: Angles, rotation and proportional time; the idealised relation between celestial-pole altitude and observer latitude.
Evidence: A coordinate diagram and a prediction with assumptions. This is an astronomy model, not a substitute for practical navigation training.

What does a changed glacier outline establish? Compare two dated, attributable images or maps of the Athabasca Glacier after checking scale and registration. Identify a defensible common reference and estimate a terminus displacement with uncertainty. A change in terminus position is not a direct measure of ice mass.
Mathematical demand: Distance / elapsed time; scale correction and an uncertainty range. Advanced work compares more dates or competing rate models.
Evidence: A reproducible overlay or tracing and an uncertainty statement. Published imagery is the default; no glacier travel is required.

How can we explain Medicine Lake? Read Parks Canada’s account, draw the visible and underground pathways, and construct a water budget. Compare seasonal inflow change with a change in drainage capacity. Mark observations separately from assumptions. Use an explicitly illustrative flow card for numerical practice.
Mathematical demand: Change in storage = total inflow minus total outflow over an interval. Track volume and time units; identify unknown terms.
Evidence: A balanced example and a list of observations needed to discriminate explanations. No dye, tracer or water collection.

Which model explains the cooling curve? Compare wrapped and unwrapped identical cups using staff-prepared warm water indoors. Record equal starting conditions and repeat measurements. Plot temperature difference from room temperature. Explain how a controlled model relates to mountain preparation and where that comparison fails.
Mathematical demand: Rates, graphs and an exponential-cooling extension using supplied logarithm tables; discuss conduction, convection and evaporation.
Evidence: Raw observations, a graph, two confounders and a justified revision. Materials and temperatures follow the staff manual.

What does Miette’s mineral list actually tell us? Use the published Parks Canada dataset: sulphate 1130, calcium 307, bicarbonate 124, magnesium 56 and sodium 10.5 mg/L. Convert a selected value into mmol/L using supplied molar masses. Compare charge equivalents and explain why the listed species may not close a complete charge balance.
Mathematical demand: Mass concentration, amount of substance, ionic charge and units. Identify measurement-date and completeness limitations.
Evidence: A transparent calculation and an explanation of why these published values are not this cohort’s field samples. No claim about drinking safety.

What would count as evidence after fire? Use sourced Jasper recovery material and a clearly labelled printed teaching grid to compare sampling plans. For a real dataset, identify dates, locations, selection and missing observations. Explain why one burned/unburned comparison cannot isolate the fire’s effect from prior differences.
Mathematical demand: Sampling bias, proportions, variability and confounding. Compare results under two sample-selection rules.
Evidence: An auditable sampling plan and a cautious interpretation. No unapproved plots, collecting or entry into closed areas.

What does gaining height cost in a model? Use a fictional mass and an approved or clearly illustrative route profile. Calculate gravitational energy and average mechanical power. Compare route choices by time, access, effort and purpose. Explain why the energy calculation is not a personal calorie prescription.
Mathematical demand: Delta E = mgh; power = energy / time; opportunity cost and sensitivity to assumptions.
Evidence: A calculation with units and a reasoned choice. No collection or publication of classmates’ body mass.

How could a useful explanation fail? Return to one water, sky, heat or glacier model. Change a stated assumption and derive a new prediction. Use a low-risk tabletop test or a fresh published observation when available. Require the other pair to challenge the prediction rather than merely repeat arithmetic.
Mathematical demand: Choose geometry, rates, concentration or uncertainty analysis appropriate to the question. Explain the model’s domain.
Evidence: A comparison of two explanations and a stated observation that could distinguish them.

What can we now investigate with intellectual honesty? Complete a scoped proposal using already approved methods or published data. State the question, source provenance, predicted result, alternative explanation, method and limitation. Keep failed trials and unresolved questions. Field research needs prior determination and authorization where required.
Mathematical demand: Select and defend a suitable model. Advanced work may compare models or test robustness; a new equation is not required.
Evidence: A documented dataset, analysis and first dossier. Label original observations, sourced records and invented exercises distinctly.

Can your explanation survive a serious question? Exchange dossiers and audit one critical calculation or method. Each learner answers questions about evidence, assumptions and alternatives, then revises the conclusion. Retain the pre-revision account for the optional AI Return Lab.
Mathematical demand: Check units, model assumptions, uncertainty and logical inference. Explain one thing the evidence cannot establish.
Evidence: Final scientific dossier and an individual defence; an impressive graphic cannot substitute for understanding.

Parks Canada reports calcium at 307 mg/L. Using 40.08 g/mol, 0.307 g/L ÷ 40.08 g/mol = 0.00766 mol/L, or about 7.66 mmol/L. As Ca2+, this corresponds to about 15.3 milliequivalents/L. This is a calculation from a published value, not a current analysis of a learner’s sample. [D4]

A teaching scenario gives inflow 2.0 m3/s and total outflow 2.5 m3/s for one hour, with other terms already included. Storage changes by (2.0 - 2.5) × 3600 = -1800 m3. These numbers are invented. A real lake-level change cannot be converted to that volume without the basin geometry.

A fictional mapped displacement of 120 ± 20 m over 10 years gives an average 12 ± 2 m/year if the dates are treated as exact. It does not reveal year-to-year variation or ice-mass loss. Real imagery needs scale, registration and dating before the same method is defensible.

blocks.text: A claim is not an authority

blocks.html: Instructor-written claims may test reasoning, but are not evidence of an AI model’s behaviour. Preserve the learner’s own explanation before the optional connected audit. Cite the actual model output, prompt and date when one is later used.
The primary-source pack identifies real data. Teaching values remain visibly labelled wherever copied into a learner’s work.

sections.title: What the cooling curve can establish

blocks.html: This worked example demonstrates reasoning. The values are synthetic teaching data, not measurements from Jasper or a learner cohort. Imagine two identical cups starting at 40°C in a 20°C room; Cup A is unwrapped and Cup B has a candidate wrap. There is one demonstration per condition.

At 20 minutes, A cooled by 40 − 28 = 12°C and B by 40 − 33.5 = 6.5°C. Their final-temperature difference is 5.5°C. Mean temperature-drop rates are 0.60 and 0.325°C/min over this interval; these averages do not establish a constant cooling rate.

Overclaim: “This wrap keeps hikers safe.” Revision: “In this synthetic, unreplicated demonstration B stays warmer over 20 minutes. We cannot isolate the wrap’s causal effect, estimate reliable variability or establish outdoor clothing performance.”

Use repeated independent trials, matched water volumes and cup geometry, calibrated thermometers, consistent timing and stable ambient conditions. Randomise cup position and record evaporation or airflow. Compare temperature above ambient; preserve all trials, including those that challenge the prediction.
n = 1 demonstration per condition. No statistical generalisation or safety recommendation follows. Actual warm-water activities require staff preparation and the manual’s handling controls.

head: Level
Task
Evidence
rows: Foundation
Calculate the two drops; label a graph and units; distinguish synthetic values from observation.
An explained calculation and one limitation.
Standard
Analyse temperature above ambient; compare interval rates; identify confounders and propose repeated trials.
A method critique and a justified revised claim.
Extension
Test an exponential-cooling model with supplied logarithm tables; examine residuals and sensitivity to ambient temperature.
Model assumptions, alternative explanation and an auditable prediction.

blocks.html: The calculation earns credit for explicit units and a reproducible method. The revised claim earns credit for separating a result from its proposed explanation. Full independence requires the learner to defend why the next test could distinguish alternatives. A polished graph alone earns no extra inference.

Keep the first claim, the strongest objection, the corrected account and the new question together. Use the same evidence pattern in a reading argument or a shared-resource decision. Publish only separately consented work, labelled accurately as educator-created or learner-produced.
These tasks fit existing science, tutorial and Commons time. They do not add hours or require a learner to choose the most mathematically advanced route to meet the introductory standard.

Read closely enough to understand a thinker, argue carefully enough to expose a weakness, and remain free enough to revise your own view. Place texts in historical and cultural context. No author or civilization represents a single timeless doctrine.

15 context and vocabulary; 30 quiet reading with optional read-aloud support; 30 reconstruct the argument; 20 paired explanation; 10 exit question. Mark claim, reason, assumption and a passage reference.

10 retrieval; 20 close reading of a disputed passage; 30 exploratory discussion; 20 present the strongest opposing position; 10 revise a sentence. The opponent must recognise their view before rebuttal begins.

15 minutes preparation; 60 in two tutorial rotations; 20 plenary comparison; 10 written revision. Two tutors each meet two pairs for 30 minutes; the other rotation is supervised writing. Each learner receives one pair tutorial weekly.

Two four-minute openings; six minutes clarifying questions; ten evidence and objections; six role reversal; five written revision. The chair protects time and fair participation. Written questions are welcome.

Prepare 3,000–5,000 core words weekly, adjusted for complexity and access. Four independent-study hours cover reading, essays and science; in-class work remains. Provide exact editions, passages and glossaries. Extension reading is optional.

Two revised essays of 1,200–1,500 words each or an equivalent: Essay 1 in Weeks 1–3; Essay 2 in Weeks 4–6. Defend a precise claim, primary passages, a serious counterargument and a justified revision. Keep tutorial notes.

Bring a written argument or essay section and two passage references. Your partner brings the strongest objection they can construct fairly. The tutor reads submitted work in preparation; this time belongs in the staffing budget.

4 minutes first learner’s claim; 4 second learner’s response; 12 tutor-led examination of text, reasoning and alternatives; 6 minutes reversing or strengthening positions; 4 minutes agreeing one substantive revision. Rotate opening roles weekly. Each person must explain their own reasoning.

During the 60-minute Day D studio, Tutor A meets pairs 1 and 2; Tutor B meets pairs 3 and 4. Each appointment lasts 30 minutes. The other pairs write under the studio’s shared supervision. A second academically competent tutor is required for one hour weekly, plus preparation; this is additional staffing, not additional learner contact hours.

In Week 6, each learner uses 15 minutes of their pair’s slot to defend their own work. The other learner may observe by agreement. Accessible written or supported responses preserve the reasoning standard. A qualified external reviewer may join if secured, with their role and conflicts disclosed.
The schedule requires the named staff and suitable space before launch. Assessment cannot depend on a promised external reviewer who has not agreed to participate.

What deserves our attention? Plato, Apology: selected passages on examination and responsibility; Laozi, Tao Te Ching: Chapters 1, 2 and 11. Compare what argument reveals with what naming may conceal.
Evidence: A 400–600-word opening argument, two annotated passages and a tutorial revision.

When does practice become character? Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1–6; Confucius, Analects 2.4, 4.17, 12.1 and 15.24. Read Dhammapada II, verses 21–32 as a short third perspective on attention and conduct.
Evidence: An Essay 1 draft connecting a precise textual claim with one observed practice; distinguish habit from conformity.
Assign bounded selections, not every complete work listed. The weekly reader, tutorial and essay stages belong to one coherent question. Readings are invitations to inquiry, not required beliefs.

Can we know and fail to act? Wang Yangming’s knowledge/action exchange recorded by Xu Ai, paired with Hume, Enquiry IV on experience and inference. Preserve their different questions and historical settings.
Evidence: Essay 1 revised to 1,200–1,500 words or equivalent; answer a counterexample in tutorial.
Who has the standing to speak? Mill, On Liberty II; Wollstonecraft, Vindication II. Examine the institutions and educational opportunities needed for meaningful independence.
Evidence: A 600–800-word Essay 2 proposal, an opposing argument represented fairly and a learner-council decision record.
Assign bounded selections, not every complete work listed. The weekly reader, tutorial and essay stages belong to one coherent question. Readings are invitations to inquiry, not required beliefs.

How should a community govern what it shares? Selected passages from Ostrom, Governing the Commons, Chapter 3, alongside Tagore, Gitanjali 35–36 and local published mapping history. Test an institutional rule against a concrete shared-resource problem.
Evidence: Essay 2 draft; a proposed rule with monitoring, revision and a fair account of who bears its costs.
What can personal agency change? Douglass, Narrative VI–VII; Epictetus, Enchiridion 1, 5 and 30. Ask what requires personal practice and what requires changing institutions.
Evidence: Essay 2 revised to 1,200–1,500 words or equivalent; individual defence and a justified continuation plan.
Assign bounded selections, not every complete work listed. The weekly reader, tutorial and essay stages belong to one coherent question. Readings are invitations to inquiry, not required beliefs.

sections.title: Make the reader ready to teach

blocks.text: A prepared reader is a launch requirement

blocks.html: The lead must record the selected edition, translation, exact passage boundaries, word count, source date, rights basis and accessible format for every week. Core reading is about 3,000–5,000 words weekly, adjusted for complexity. Guided reading also occurs in class; reading, essays and science share four independent-study hours weekly.

Weeks 1–6 address attention, discipline, evidence, freedom, responsibility and contribution. Preserve real differences between authors. Primary arguments are studied in context, not reduced to a common slogan or compulsory belief.
Legends of Vancouver. Author’s foreword and The Siwash Rock. Specified Gutenberg source. Source edition.

Johnson’s account remains an extension or back-catalogue resource, not an extra compulsory Week 5 reading. Any new selection must have a clear question, sufficient teaching time and verified reuse arrangements. Ibn Khaldun and further traditions belong in later carefully designed sequences.

Number passages; provide readable type, a glossary, source notes and prompt sheets. Retain historical context and identify translation choices. The academic lead signs off the actual pack before formal applications open; this curriculum does not contain a complete anthology.
Public access to a text, public-domain status in another country and permission to reproduce a modern translation are different questions. Verify the actual edition and intended Canadian use.
Make knowledge useful. Each week: a 75-minute workshop, 45-minute project clinic and 60-minute review. Rotate convenor, recorder, materials steward, access reviewer and critic.

blocks.text: Week 1 / A charter for working together

blocks.html: A learner council decides discussion norms, shared duties and an approved project choice. Record dissent and revisions. Staff retain safety, complaint, employment and financial responsibilities. Choose an inquiry and begin the portfolio.

blocks.text: Week 2 / The cost of a choice

blocks.html: Workshop: allocate a fictional fixed resource budget. Clinic: compare time, materials and access costs. Review: examine who loses an opportunity when a choice is made. Output: an explicit opportunity-cost account; no real spending is required.

Workshop: exchange incomplete experiments and identify the most useful criticism. Clinic: choose a prototype. Review: name what failed and revise one method. Output: a prototype brief with an honest evidence boundary.

blocks.text: Week 4 / A claim deserves a test

blocks.html: Test the proposed capstone against evidence or a primary argument. The council allocates presentation time or another approved non-financial resource. Assign a sceptical peer and a testable plan. AI comparison follows after the semester.

A confirmed host may define a useful task; otherwise work with a consenting peer. Test an explanation, source guide or shared-resource proposal and label feedback honestly. No recovery work, construction or partnership is promised without agreement.
Workshop: prepare the final evidence table. Clinic: rehearse the oral defence. Review: present, challenge and revise. Output: a portable portfolio, useful artefact and voluntary 30-day continuation.

In pairs, investigate one question that joins physical experience, scientific reasoning and a human judgment. Produce a paper artefact usable by a consenting peer or confirmed local host. Every learner also explains their own reasoning independently.

blocks.text: Examples with a real intellectual demand

blocks.html: A packing guide based on a controlled heat-retention comparison; an accessible route-decision worksheet using scale, grade and uncertainty; a fair-use plan for shared camp materials with an opportunity-cost analysis; or a philosophical reader that makes a genuine disagreement understandable. No unapproved construction, environmental sampling or human health research.

One-page question and context; relevant source passages; original raw data or documented observations; a model or argument; limitations and a competing explanation; artefact versions 1 and 2; a record of consenting feedback; cost/access consequences; individual contribution statements.

blocks.text: Final Day D commons session: 60 minutes

blocks.html: 5 minutes opening. Up to four pairs receive 10 minutes each: 3 demonstration, 3 evidence questions, 2 individual questions (one minute per learner) and 2 revision summary. Use the remaining 15 minutes for private feedback and a next-step commitment. With three pairs, use spare time for deeper critique.

Science Investigation 12 and the Week 6 tutorial assess each learner independently. Invite a qualified external reviewer when one is secured; disclose their role and conflicts. The final Commons Hearing may become a public showcase with participants’ separate consent and a confirmed host, using the existing 60-minute session.

Use the five-dimension rubric, plus the instructor-reviewed field and martial demonstrations. “Original” means a genuine question, choice or revision by the learner, not a claim of a globally novel discovery. Intellectual honesty is essential.
The work must be useful, inspectable and proportionate to six weeks of learning. A modest result explained well is stronger than an impressive claim that cannot be defended.

sections.eyebrow: OPTIONAL AFTER THE SEMESTER / THREE HOURS
sections.title: Return to AI Keep your judgment

blocks.html: An optional connected laboratory examines AI using work the learner produced offline. It follows the six-week core and is separately scheduled, staffed and resourced. It is not a compulsory seventh week or part of the 168-hour academic workload.

Choose a non-sensitive calculation, argument or design from the preserved portfolio. Record your own answer and a criterion for improvement before viewing the model’s response. Participation and sharing are optional.

20 minutes select work and define criteria; 20 write and record a prompt; 35 inspect output; 45 verify consequential claims using sources or data; 30 revise independently; 20 compare accounts with a peer; 10 write a decision about future use. Record model, date, prompt, output and any tool access.

A four-column audit: original work; model contribution; verification; final judgment. Identify a learner error, a model error if found, and an unresolved uncertainty. Disclose assistance. A model that helps one task may fail another.
Use the same task and criteria; separate tool-assisted verification from the model’s unaided answer. Do not infer broad model rankings, human superiority or causation from a small classroom exercise.

No account purchase or data upload is required by this proposal. A facilitator can prepare an attributed, permission-cleared example for those who do not use an account. No private learner or third-party data should be entered into an external tool without appropriate permission.
